For an eigenvalue \(\lambda\), the three steps multiply that component by
\[
p(\lambda)=\prod_{k=0}^2(1-\alpha_k\lambda).
\]
Since \(A\) is real symmetric, the worst case over \(A\) and \(x_0\) is exactly
\[
R(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=\max_{\lambda\in[1,9]} |p(\lambda)|.
\]

We claim the optimum is attained at
\[
(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=\left(\frac{65}{389},\frac29,\frac29\right).
\]
For this choice,
\[
p(\lambda)=\left(1-\frac{65}{389}\lambda\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{9}\lambda\right)^2.
\]
At the endpoints,
\[
p(1)=\frac{324}{389}\cdot\frac{49}{81}=\frac{196}{389},
\]
and
\[
p(9)=\left(1-\frac{585}{389}\right)(-1)^2=-\frac{196}{389}.
\]
The derivative is
\[
p'(\lambda)=-\left(1-\frac{2\lambda}{9}\right)
\left(\frac{65}{389}+\frac49-\frac{260}{3501}\lambda\right),
\]
so the only interior critical points are \(\lambda=9/2\) and
\[
\lambda=\frac{2141}{390}.
\]
At \(\lambda=9/2\), \(p=0\), and at \(\lambda=2141/390\) the value is positive and smaller than \(p(1)\). Thus
\[
\max_{\lambda\in[1,9]}|p(\lambda)|=\frac{196}{389}.
\]

It remains to prove no smaller value is possible. If \(\alpha_0\le 1/9\), then since \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\le2/9\),
\[
R\ge p(1)=\prod_{k=0}^2(1-\alpha_k)
\ge \frac89\left(\frac79\right)^2
=\frac{392}{729}
>\frac{196}{389}.
\]
So any optimizer with smaller or equal value must have all \(\alpha_k>1/9\). Put
\[
y_k=9\alpha_k-1\in(0,1].
\]
Then
\[
|p(9)|=\prod_{k=0}^2 y_k=:Y,
\]
while
\[
p(1)=\prod_{k=0}^2\left(1-\alpha_k\right)
=\frac1{729}\prod_{k=0}^2(8-y_k).
\]
For \(x,y\in(0,1]\),
\[
(8-x)(8-y)\ge 7(8-xy),
\]
because the difference is
\[
(8-x)(8-y)-7(8-xy)=8(1-x)(1-y)\ge0.
\]
Applying this twice gives
\[
\prod_{k=0}^2(8-y_k)\ge 49(8-Y).
\]
Therefore
\[
R\ge \max\left(Y,\frac{49(8-Y)}{729}\right).
\]
The first term increases in \(Y\), the second decreases in \(Y\), so the best possible lower bound occurs when they are equal:
\[
Y=\frac{49(8-Y)}{729}.
\]
Hence
\[
778Y=392,
\qquad
Y=\frac{196}{389}.
\]
Thus every admissible triple satisfies
\[
R(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)\ge \frac{196}{389}.
\]
Equality in the inequality forces two of the \(y_k\)'s to equal \(1\), and the remaining one to equal \(196/389\). Since the \(\alpha_k\) are ordered, this gives uniquely
\[
\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\frac29,
\qquad
9\alpha_0-1=\frac{196}{389},
\]
so
\[
\alpha_0=\frac{65}{389}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\left(R_*,(\alpha_0^*,\alpha_1^*,\alpha_2^*)\right)
=\left(\frac{196}{389},\left(\frac{65}{389},\frac29,\frac29\right)\right)}
\]
